paras: The attempted lynching in Chippewa County, Wisconsin, was an attempt by a crowd in that county to lynch an unnamed young man, who escaped from them, at some time before April 1881. It is known only from a news brief on the Wisconsin House of Representatives' rejection of a bill to restore the death penalty, which named the attempt as the origin of that effort.

The coverage gives no date, town, name, race or accusation for the attempt. According to the brief, "a Chippewa county crowd" tried "to lynch a young man who finally got away from them." Nothing in the text describes whether he was seized, where the crowd gathered or how he escaped.

The brief presented the attempt as the starting point of the campaign to "re-establish capital punishment" in Wisconsin. That campaign failed in the House, by a vote printed as 51 to 22 in one copy and 51 to 52 in the other. No report of arrests or charges against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The Portland Daily Press carried the two-sentence item on April 4, 1881, and the Daily Kennebec Journal of Augusta, Maine, ran it in nearly the same words two days later. Both papers treated the attempted lynching as background to a legislative vote rather than as news, and neither commented on the crowd. No Wisconsin report of the attempt itself was found, and Black-press coverage for the period is not available.

bases: Both copies of the brief describe an attempt by a Chippewa County crowd to lynch a young man who escaped, an attempted lynching (A3, A4).

The young man 'finally got away' from the crowd, so no one was killed (A3, A4); the brief gives no accusation, crowd size or race, so the attempt cannot be tested further against the standard definition.
The only two reports are near-identical copies of one brief that ran two days apart in Maine papers (A3, A4); no first-hand or Wisconsin report of the attempt was found.
